title: Identify, discuss, describe and compare major economic systems, with emphasis on the South African economy

lessons.title: Three main economic systems
lessons.html:
What is an economic system?

Every country must answer three questions: What must we produce? How must we produce it? Who gets the goods? The way a country answers these questions is called its economic system.

Market economy (free market)

In a market economy, people and private businesses own the farms, factories and shops. They decide what to grow and sell. Prices are set by buyers and sellers. If many people want tomatoes, the price goes up and farmers plant more tomatoes. The government does not control much.

  • Good: people are free to start businesses; there is lots of choice.
  • Bad: some people become very rich and others stay poor.

Command economy (planned economy)

In a command economy the government owns most land and businesses. The government decides what to produce, how much, and at what price. Workers may be told where to work.

  • Good: the government can make sure everyone gets basic goods.
  • Bad: there is often little choice, and shortages happen when plans are wrong.

Mixed economy

A mixed economy combines the two. Private people own most businesses, but the government also owns some important businesses and makes rules to protect people. Most countries in the world today have a mixed economy.

Traditional economy

In some rural areas people still live by a traditional economy. Families grow food and keep cattle the way their parents did. Goods may be swapped instead of bought with money. Cattle in the kraal are a store of wealth.

Think about your own village. Which system do you see when your family sells a goat, buys mealie meal at the shop, or gets a social grant?

lessons.title: The South African economy
lessons.html:
South Africa has a mixed economy

In South Africa most farms, shops, mines and factories are owned by private people and companies. Farmers decide whether to grow maize, citrus or keep sheep, and prices are mostly set by the market. But the government also plays a big role. That is why we say South Africa has a mixed economy.

What the government does

  • Owns or controls some big state-owned companies, such as Eskom (electricity) and Transnet (rail and ports).
  • Makes laws, for example minimum wages for farm workers and rules on food safety.
  • Collects tax through SARS and uses it for schools, clinics, roads and social grants.
  • Supports farmers through the Department of Agriculture with advice and some programmes.

The main sectors

SectorExamples
PrimaryFarming, fishing, forestry, mining
SecondaryFactories, food processing, building
TertiaryShops, banks, transport, tourism

Farming is a primary sector. It produces food for the country and also exports fruit, wine and wool to other countries, which brings in foreign money.

Challenges

South Africa has high unemployment and big gaps between rich and poor. Many people in rural areas have little land. Drought, power cuts and high fuel prices also hurt farmers. Land reform and job creation programmes try to deal with some of these problems.

Comparing the systems

A pure market economy would leave everything to business. A pure command economy would leave everything to the government. South Africa sits in between, trying to keep the freedom of the market while protecting workers and the poor.

Key points

  • An economic system answers: what, how and for whom to produce.
  • A market economy is run by private owners and prices; a command economy by the government.
  • A mixed economy combines both; South Africa has a mixed economy.
  • Farming is part of the primary sector and earns money from exports.
  • Unemployment and inequality are big challenges in South Africa.
